reasoning: Nothing clears the bar this week, and the account stays flat. (1) Oil: crude is pricing a binary outcome, a peace deal or continued attacks on Hormuz shipping. The Nov 3 marks are already $8-10 stale, so entry at the next official mark would come after a large, unknowable gap, and a stop tight enough to keep risk sensible would sit inside the daily noise. That leaves no edge in either direction (sources: tradingeconomics.com/commodity/crude-oil/news/598646; theglobeandmail.com/investing/article-oil-tumbles-as-investors-weigh-end-to-iran-war-after-us-democrats/; unitedagainstnucleariran.com/analysis/iran-shipping-update-november-5-2026). (2) US10Y: a lower oil price argues for a bond rally. Against that, the Fed has a hiking bias, with two dissents for a hike and a strong 55.5 ISM manufacturing reading. The 15bp fall in yields over the past week has already priced part of the oil move (sources: cnbc.com/2026/10/28/fed-interest-rate-decision-october-2026.html; seekingalpha.com/article/4958991). (3) JPY: there are arguments for a long. The US and Japan have intervened jointly before, and cheaper oil helps Japan's terms of trade. But MUFG notes persistent structural outflows and a weak link between rate gaps and the yen, and negative carry against a hiking Fed eats into any payoff. My honest probability is about 52%, which is not worth paying costs for (sources: tradingpedia.com/2026/11/04/yen-climbs-on-intervention-fears-softer-dollar/; tmgm.com MUFG yen note). (4) FR-DE: the spread could tighten further from 150bp or widen sharply again depending on the budget vote. I have no informational edge on that vote (source: pandaequityresearch.substack.com/p/the-spread-is-only-the-first-price). Finally, I used up my search budget before I could check the BoE decision, October payrolls, the BoJ and the ECB. Without those, I can't judge gilts, sterling, the euro, the Bund, the Swiss franc, the Aussie or the Canadian dollar. I will look again next week, once oil and the data have settled.

thesis: The 10y has fallen about 40bp in a month on lower oil and peace hopes, and a December hike is largely priced, so a benign October CPI could extend the rally into the 8-9 Dec FOMC. After The Opposition (December hike odds about 84%, not 94%; strong labour data) my view is about even, so size is the minimum needed to keep C06's two-position floor.

opposition.case_against: The thesis rests on a stale number. The 94% December-hike probability comes from the 14 October Citi/FedWatch note that followed the hot September CPI. Trading Economics puts December odds at about 84% on 10 November, up from about 74% a week earlier, and they fell as low as about 68-77% around the midterms. Hawkish repricing still has room to run, and the move is already in that direction. The labour data argue against a benign path: October payrolls were +165K against a 65K forecast, unemployment fell to 4.1%, jobless claims are at a 57-year low, productivity beat, and markets already price a further hike in 2027. The 10y depends on that terminal path, not only on the December decision. Inflation momentum is also adverse. September headline CPI was 3.7% (expected 3.6%) and core rose from 2.4% to 2.6% with a 0.3% m/m print, so price pressure is spreading beyond energy. The consensus for October already expects easing, which means a benign print is largely priced, while a core miss gets the trade stopped out. The oil leg is the weakest part. The 10y has already dropped about 40bp from 5.28% on peace hopes, yet in 2026 alone a June interim deal and a ceasefire collapsed, the August talks stalled over Iran's insistence on controlling and tolling Hormuz, and ships are still being attacked near the Strait. Finally, entry sits on the day CPI is released (10 November) with PPI on 13 November and the FOMC on 8-9 December. The stop is only 22-24bp away, well inside a normal one-month 1-sd 10y move of about 35-40bp at current vol, so the trade can be stopped out on noise even if the thesis turns out right.

thesis: Gilt yields are retreating from near-2007 highs as oil falls, and a 5%+ yield already discounts several further BoE hikes after the 5 Nov move to 4.0%. The Opposition's case (heavy fiscal supply, BoE hawkish guidance in December) leaves my view about even, so size is the minimum to meet C06's two-position floor.

opposition.case_against: The thesis is mostly priced in already. Brent has dropped from about $113 (29 Oct) to about $90 (9-10 Nov), and the 10y has rallied about 33bp in a month, to 5.11% on 10 Nov, its lowest since late August. Taking 'peace hopes' from here needs an actual deal, and this year an interim US-Iran deal already collapsed over the summer, while every round of talks has swung Brent by $5-10 on headlines. The BoE was explicit on 5 Nov that more tightening may be needed 'unless the war in Iran is resolved'. It projects CPI peaking at 4.9% in Q2 2027 (6.2% in the adverse case), with September core and services CPI above forecast. So October CPI (mid-November), labour data and Q3 GDP (Thursday, consensus a strong 0.7%) can all reprice the three further hikes the market expects by November 2027. Gilts are also following Treasuries: after a strong US jobs report, a December Fed hike is about 77-80% priced, which pulled gilt yields back above 5.15% on 6 Nov, so US CPI today and the FOMC are outside risks. The horizon also covers the December BoE meeting, where hawkish guidance would hit the trade directly. Fiscal headroom was cut from £24bn to £15bn in the 28 Oct budget, so supply and term premium are still a weak spot. Finally, the risk plan doesn't add up: the stop is at 5.40% but the stated change of mind is a close above 5.30%. The stop sits about 28bp away, roughly one month of recent realised movement (5.44 to 5.11 since late September), against a target that is never stated.
key_risks: Oil rebound: talks stall, Hormuz flows are disrupted again, or the Saudi-Iran front escalates. The summer interim deal already failed, and Brent moves $5-10 on single headlines.
Hot UK data: October CPI (with services or core still above forecast), wage data, or Q3 GDP at or above 0.7% would bring forward more BoE hikes.
December BoE meeting falls inside the horizon. Bailey's 'more tightening unless Iran is resolved' guidance is still in place, and the 8-1 vote shows no dovish group to restrain it.
US spillover: a December Fed hike is about 80% priced after strong payrolls, and a hot US CPI would lift global yields. Gilts already followed Treasuries higher on 6 Nov.
Fiscal and supply: headroom is down to £15bn, gilt issuance stays heavy, and the 6-month QT sales pause announced in September is temporary.
Mean reversion: a 33bp rally in a month into the bottom of a 5.1-5.44% range leaves little left to gain. Entering after the move gives poor reward for the risk.
Process: the stop (5.40%) and the change-of-mind level (5.30% close) disagree, and no target is set, so expected value can't be judged against the claimed 55%.
